Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: What basic facts of a financial transaction are specifically described by an accounting document according to the chapter?
Option A: Future market value, inflation rate, and vendor profit margin
Option B: Banker's specimen signature and income tax clearance certificate
Option C: Amount, recipient, purpose, and date of transaction
Option D: Depreciation rate, scrap value, and salvage estimate
Hint: Look at the four fundamental factual elements listed in the introduction of Section 6.1.
Explanation: The chapter opens by defining accounting documents as describing all basic facts of transactions: the amount of transaction, to whom the amount was paid, the purpose of transaction, and the date of transaction. The other options refer to valuation or taxation concepts not in this definition.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: What primary evidentiary role do accounting documents play in the process of Book-Keeping?
Option A: They eliminate the requirement to maintain a journal or ledger
Option B: They act as negotiable credit instruments enforceable on demand
Option C: They provide evidence that a financial transaction has actually taken place
Option D: They serve as legal authority to alter audited financial statements
Hint: Consider why an accountant insists on having bills, receipts, or vouchers before passing entries.
Explanation: The text explicitly states: 'This is essential in the process of Book Keeping as it provides evidence that a financial transaction has actually taken place.' They do not replace journals or ledgers, nor do they permit altering audited books.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Which modern banking method provides instant and automatic proof of payment and receipt for both parties without requiring a physical visit to the bank?
Option A: Manual withdrawal slip
Option B: Internet and mobile banking
Option C: Over-the-counter pay-in-slip
Option D: Postal clearing slip
Hint: Identify the electronic banking channel highlighted in Section 6.1 that creates immediate digital records.
Explanation: Section 6.1 explains that internet and mobile banking play a prominent role in modern business because payments and receipts of cash through these methods generate instant and automatic proof for both parties.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: What is another commonly used name for a Pay-in-slip?
Option A: Withdrawal slip
Option B: Deposit slip
Option C: Credit note
Option D: Bank advice
Hint: Think of the document filled out when putting money into an account.
Explanation: Under 'Types of Bank Documents (1)', the text states: 'Pay-in-slip is also known as deposit slip. This slip is filled when the account holder deposits cheque or cash into his bank account.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: A Pay-in-slip is divided into two parts. Which part is stamped, signed, dated by the receiving clerk, and returned to the customer as an acknowledgement?
Option A: The bank's internal clearing voucher
Option B: The micro-perforated carbon copy
Option C: The left-hand side counterfoil
Option D: The right-hand side portion
Hint: Identify the specific term used for the customer's retention side of the slip.
Explanation: The chapter explains that a pay-in-slip is divided into two parts: the right-hand side is kept with the bank for their record, while the left-hand side, known as the counterfoil, is duly stamped, signed, dated by the clerk, and returned to the account holder as acknowledgement.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Why is the counterfoil of a pay-in-slip vital for the business accountant?
Option A: It guarantees that the deposited cheque will never be dishonoured
Option B: It allows the account holder to withdraw cash without filling a withdrawal form
Option C: It replaces the need for maintaining a Cash Book bank column
Option D: It acts as legal evidence and forms the source document to record bank deposits in the books of accounts
Hint: Focus on the dual utilities of the counterfoil: source document for book entries and legal proof.
Explanation: Under 'Importance and Utilities' of pay-in-slip: (ii) Entries in respect of cash or cheque deposited are recorded in the books of accounts on the basis of pay-in-slip, and (iii) Counterfoil acts as legal evidence. It does not prevent cheque bounce or eliminate the Cash Book.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Under statutory banking guidelines shown in the Pay-in-slip format, quoting a PAN card number is compulsory when cash deposit exceeds what amount?
Hint: Recall the monetary limit specified in the pay-in-slip specimen for cash deposits.
Explanation: Contents item (x) and the pay-in-slip specimen explicitly specify: 'PAN card number if the amount of deposit is more than 50,000' (or For Cash Deposit of 50,000 & Above).

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Which detail of cash currency must be specified on a pay-in-slip when depositing physical currency into a bank account?
Option A: Breakdown of denominations, specifying the count of Rs 100, Rs 200, Rs 500, and Rs 2000 notes
Option B: Serial numbers of every individual currency note deposited
Option C: The signature of the Reserve Bank Governor on each note
Option D: The year in which the currency notes were minted or printed
Hint: Think of the cash denomination table printed on the slip.
Explanation: Contents item (vii) of Pay-in-slip states: 'Details of denomination, i.e. number of Rs 100, Rs 200, Rs 500, Rs 2000 notes etc. deposited.' Serial numbers or mint dates are not required.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: How can a customer deposit a cheque along with a pay-in-slip in modern branches without waiting at the teller counter?
Option A: By sending a certified SMS to the branch manager
Option B: By attaching it to a withdrawal form at the ATM
Option C: By dropping it into the designated drop box placed in the bank
Option D: By submitting an online RTGS application form
Hint: Look for the note directly following Fig. 6.1(a) on page 179.
Explanation: The chapter notes: 'In modern times, a cheque along with duly filled pay-in-slip can be simply dropped into the drop box placed in the bank for collection.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: What is a Withdrawal Slip, and how does its record availability differ from a pay-in-slip?
Option A: It is an electronic statement emailed to the account holder each quarter
Option B: It is a form filled for withdrawing money from bank; a retained copy is not available to the customer, but the entry is reflected in the Pass Book
Option C: It is a slip issued by the clearing house confirming cheque dishonour
Option D: It is a negotiable instrument that provides a counterfoil to record entries in the Cash Book
Hint: Notice the explicit sentence about document copies under 'Withdrawal Slip: Meaning' on page 179.
Explanation: The text states: 'Form which is to be filled for withdrawing money from bank is known as withdrawal slip or form. A copy of this document is not available to record the transaction in the books of accounts but it is reflected in the Pass Book.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Which of the following restrictions applies to the use of a cash withdrawal slip according to its printed conditions?
Option A: It can be endorsed to third-party suppliers as payment for goods
Option B: It can be presented at any branch of any scheduled commercial bank nationwide
Option C: It can be used only when the account has an authorized overdraft limit
Option D: It is not a cheque, must accompany the Pass Book, and can be used at the home branch only
Hint: Read the notices printed across the top of the cash withdrawal slip format (Fig. 6.1b).
Explanation: The specimen format specifically states: 'Pass Book must accompany with this withdrawal. Please sign overleaf. This withdrawal slip is not a cheque. Use at home branch only.' Distractors A and C contradict these explicit rules.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Why must an account holder sign both on the face and on the reverse side of a withdrawal slip?
Option A: To convert the form into a multi-currency draft
Option B: To authorise the bank to debit standing orders and bank commission
Option C: To waive the customer's right to receive a Bank Statement
Option D: To allow the teller to match the signature with specimen signatures in the bank's records, preventing malpractices
Hint: Consider the verification procedure performed by the bank clerk before disbursing cash.
Explanation: Under Utilities of Withdrawal Slip: 'Account holder signs on the face of the slip and backside of the slip. Signature of the account holder is matched with his/her specimen signature recorded in the books of bank thereby avoiding malpractices.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: When cash withdrawal using a withdrawal slip exceeds Rs 50,000, what additional document must be submitted by the account holder?
Option A: Photocopy of their PAN card
Option B: Duplicate copy of the current month's Cash Book
Option C: A registered mortgage deed
Option D: A written indemnity bond counter-signed by an auditor
Hint: Recall the tax identification document required for high-value banking transactions.
Explanation: The text states: 'If the amount of withdrawal is more than 50,000 account holder has to submit a photocopy of his PAN card.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: What is the specific term used in the chapter for availing banking services through extensive use of information technology without physically walking into bank premises?
Option A: Branch clearing banking
Option B: Merchant banking
Option C: Virtual banking
Option D: Consortium banking
Hint: Look at the definition highlighted in the boxed callout on page 180.
Explanation: The text defines: 'Availing banking services through an extensive use of information technology without physically walking into the bank premises is called virtual banking.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: What is a Bank Pass Book fundamentally defined as?
Option A: A copy or extract of the ledger account of the account holder appearing in the books of the bank
Option B: A daily clearing memo issued by the Reserve Bank of India
Option C: A statutory register maintaining details of shareholders' equity
Option D: A duplicate of the cash column of the business Cash Book
Hint: Notice whose books it is an extract of, and whose account it details.
Explanation: Section 6.1(3) defines Pass Book as: 'a copy or extract of ledger account of account holder appearing in the books of bank. In this the bank provides the account holder with the details of all ledger entries appearing in the books of bank.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: During which century did Bank Pass Books first appear, giving customers transaction records in their own hands?
Option A: 19th century
Option B: 18th century
Option C: 20th century
Option D: 15th century
Hint: Check the historical note at the end of Section 6.1(3) on page 181.
Explanation: The chapter mentions: 'Pass Books appeared in the 18th century, allowing customers to have transaction information in their own hands for the first time. Prior to this, customers had no history of their own deposits and withdrawals.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: What is the nature and purpose of IFSC as detailed in a Bank Pass Book?
Option A: It is a secret four-digit PIN code used to authorize ATM cash withdrawals
Option B: It is a barcode printed exclusively to calculate monthly interest charges
Option C: It is a 16-digit purely numeric code verifying international credit ratings
Option D: It is an alphanumeric code that facilitates electronic funds transfer like IMPS, NEFT, and RTGS
Hint: Focus on the code's composition (letters and numbers) and its fund transfer facilitation role.
Explanation: Under Contents of Pass Book: 'IFSC (Indian Financial System Code) It is an alphanumeric code that facilitates electronic funds transfer like IMPS, NEFT and RTGS.' It is not a secret PIN or credit rating code.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Why do commercial banks provide a periodic Bank Statement instead of a Pass Book to Current Account holders?
Option A: Because current accounts cannot legally be recorded in computerized banking systems
Option B: Because current accounts have zero deposits and are restricted to government transactions
Option C: Because Bank Statements are only issued when an account runs into overdraft
Option D: Because businessmen enjoy unlimited deposits and withdrawals, resulting in a large volume of transactions best summarised periodically
Hint: Consider the frequency and volume of transactions conducted by business firms.
Explanation: The text explains under Section 6.1(4): 'Current account holders enjoy unlimited number of deposits and withdrawals and therefore the number of transactions is large. Businessmen like to know the details of transactions and the bank balance. Therefore, the bank issues a bank statement to them.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: What direct operational and financial benefit does viewing, downloading, and printing electronic bank statements offer to banks and account holders?
Option A: It reduces the cost of paper and postage
Option B: It prevents cheques from being dishonoured
Option C: It guarantees an interest-free overdraft facility
Option D: It eliminates the need to maintain an internal Cash Book
Hint: Look for the specific cost-saving advantage cited on page 181.
Explanation: The chapter states: 'Today with better access to the internet and online banking, bank statement also known as electronic statement can be viewed online, downloaded and printed by the account holder. This reduces the cost of paper and postage.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: What is a 'Bank Advice' as explained in the chapter?
Option A: A letter sent by the bank to an account holder in a prescribed form to inform them of debits/credits like dishonour, bank charges, or standing order payments
Option B: A formal notice served by tax authorities freezing an account
Option C: A letter sent by a customer requesting the bank to increase overdraft limits
Option D: A loan sanction letter detailing mortgage terms
Hint: Notice who sends the advice to whom and for what accounting purposes.
Explanation: Section 6.1(5) defines Bank Advice as: 'a letter sent by the bank to customer / account holder in a prescribed form to inform them about dishonour of cheques... bank charges debited, dishonour of Bills receivable discounted... interest charged and allowed... dividend collected... and payments made according to standing instructions.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Which contemporary technology has largely overtaken the role of physical Bank Advices for updating account holders?
Option A: Telegram dispatches
Option B: Bank passbook drop boxes
Option C: Monthly certified post receipts
Option D: SMS alerts and notifications on registered mobile numbers
Hint: Recall what message arrives instantly on a mobile phone after making a transaction.
Explanation: The chapter highlights: 'SMS alerts and notifications have overtaken bank advice today. Account holder receives SMS on their registered mobile number giving updates of their latest banking transactions.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Which electronic funds transfer system is available 24/7 throughout the year, including bank holidays, for immediate fund transfers?
Option A: Demand Draft (DD)
Option B: Immediate Payment Service (IMPS)
Option C: Cheque Clearing House
Option D: Physical Pay Order
Hint: Look for the instant payment interbank service mentioned in the callout on page 186.
Explanation: The text explains: 'IMPS (Immediate Payment Service) is an instant payment interbank electronic funds transfer system in India. When an account holder needs to transfer funds immediately, IMPS can be used because this service is available 24/7 throughout the year including bank holidays.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: According to the chapter, for which transfer amounts are NEFT and RTGS respectively considered suitable?
Option A: NEFT is suitable for transfers greater than Rs 10 Lakhs, while RTGS is for transfers up to Rs 50,000
Option B: NEFT is suitable only for international transfers, while RTGS is for local branch deposits
Option C: NEFT is suitable for transfers less than Rs 2 Lakhs, while RTGS is suitable for larger transfers greater than Rs 2 Lakhs
Option D: NEFT is suitable for cash withdrawals, while RTGS is exclusively for cheques
Hint: Recall the monetary dividing line of Rs 2 Lakhs cited on page 186.
Explanation: The chapter states: 'NEFT (National Electronic Funds Transfer) is suitable for small money transfers (less than 2 Lakhs) and RTGS (Real Time Gross Settlement) is suitable for larger money transfers (greater than 2 Lakhs).'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: In a business ledger, what does the bank column of the Cash Book represent?
Option A: The capital account contributed by partners
Option B: Physical cash in hand kept in the office safe
Option C: The bank current account maintained by the businessman
Option D: The loans and advances ledger of suppliers
Hint: Look at the definition in Section 6.2 explaining the Cash Book with bank column.
Explanation: Section 6.2 states: 'A businessman maintains a Cash Book with bank column in his ledger, wherein he records all banking transactions. The bank column in his Cash Book represents bank current account.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: When a businessman deposits money or cheques into the bank, how is the entry recorded in the Cash Book and Pass Book respectively?
Option A: Debit side of Cash Book and Debit side of Pass Book
Option B: Credit side of Cash Book (Payment) and Debit side of Pass Book (Payment)
Option C: Credit side of Cash Book and Credit side of Pass Book
Option D: Debit side of Cash Book (Receipt) and Credit side of Pass Book (Receipt)
Hint: To the firm, bank is a debit receipt; to the bank, the customer deposit is a credit liability.
Explanation: The chapter states: 'When businessman deposits money or cheque into bank for collection it is recorded in the Cash Book on the debit or receipt side. Bank records this on the credit or receipt side of Pass Book.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: When a businessman issues a cheque to pay a supplier, on which side of the Cash Book and Pass Book is the transaction entered?
Option A: Debit side of Cash Book and Credit side of Pass Book
Option B: Debit side of Cash Book and Debit side of Pass Book
Option C: Credit side of Cash Book (Payment) and Debit side of Pass Book (Payment)
Option D: Credit side of Cash Book and Credit side of Pass Book
Hint: Payment reduces the firm's bank asset (credit) and reduces the bank's liability to the customer (debit).
Explanation: Section 6.2 states: 'Similarly, when businessman issues cheque for making payments, it is recorded on the credit or payment side of Cash Book. Bank records this transaction on the debit side or payment side of Pass Book / bank statement.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Under ideal conditions with no pending differences or errors, what is the reciprocal relationship between the balances of Cash Book and Pass Book?
Option A: If the Cash Book has a debit balance, the Pass Book will have an equal credit balance, and vice versa
Option B: Both books will reflect a debit balance of equal amount
Option C: Both books will reflect a credit balance of equal amount
Option D: The Pass Book balance will always be exactly double the Cash Book balance
Hint: Remember that the two books record mirror perspectives of the same transactions.
Explanation: The chapter states: 'Ideally then, Cash Book bank balance and Pass Book balance should be the same. The only difference would be that if Cash Book has a debit balance the Pass Book will have a credit balance and vice versa.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Which of the following defines a 'Bank Reconciliation Statement' according to the chapter?
Option A: A letter sent by the bank manager detailing interest rate adjustments
Option B: A statement showing the causes of disagreement between the balance shown by the bank Pass Book and the balance shown by the Cash Book under the bank column at the end of a specific period
Option C: A journal voucher used to write off irrecoverable debts from customers
Option D: A statutory balance sheet prepared by commercial banks for regulatory audits
Hint: Look for the formal definition provided in Section 6.2.
Explanation: Section 6.2 defines BRS as: 'A statement showing the causes of disagreement between the balance shown by the bank Pass Book and the balance shown by the Cash Book under the bank column at the end of the specific period or month, is called Bank Reconciliation Statement.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Who is responsible for preparing the Bank Reconciliation Statement?
Option A: The statutory government tax auditor
Option B: The businessman / account holder
Option C: The commercial bank holding the account
Option D: The Reserve Bank of India clearing house
Hint: Exercise Q.4(5): 'Bank Reconciliation Statement is prepared by...'
Explanation: BRS is prepared by the businessman (account holder) to reconcile internal Cash Book records with the bank statement received from the bank. The bank does not prepare a BRS for individual account holders.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Which of the following is NOT an advantage or need for preparing a Bank Reconciliation Statement listed in Section 6.2?
Option A: It serves as an important mechanism of internal check and provides information on cash inflows and outflows
Option B: It helps in detecting errors and omissions made in Pass Book and Cash Book
Option C: It permanently exempts the business entity from external audits and tax liabilities
Option D: It reduces the chance of fraud by staff dealing in cash
Hint: Look for an unrealistic legal/tax claim that has nothing to do with internal financial control.
Explanation: Section 6.2 lists six reasons for the need and importance of BRS: explaining disagreements, detecting errors, reducing fraud, checking bank entries, moral check on staff, and acting as an internal check mechanism. It does NOT exempt any firm from audit or taxation.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: How does regular preparation of a BRS exercise a 'moral check' on the accounting staff of a business?
Option A: It guarantees annual bonuses to all accounting clerks
Option B: It encourages staff to keep Cash Book records accurate and up to date because omissions and misappropriations will be promptly revealed
Option C: It transfers disciplinary powers from the employer to the commercial bank
Option D: It allows clerks to record personal household expenses in the business ledger
Hint: Think of how transparent reconciliation deters negligence and dishonesty among cash-handling employees.
Explanation: Under Need and Importance item (v): 'It helps to have a moral check on the staff of business organisations to keep Cash Book up to date' and (iii) reduces the chance of fraud by staff dealing in cash.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: What are the two major broad categories of reasons causing differences between Cash Book balance and Pass Book balance?
Option A: Capital expenditures, and revenue expenditures
Option B: Time difference, and Errors and omissions made by bank or businessman
Option C: Currency exchange rate fluctuations, and trade discounts
Option D: Bad debts written off, and provision for depreciation
Hint: Refer to the main classification heading in Section 6.3 and Figure 6.3(a).
Explanation: Section 6.3 divides the reasons for difference into two categories: 'i) Time difference' and 'ii) Errors and omission made by businessman or bank.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: When a cheque is issued to a creditor but has NOT yet been presented to the bank for payment by the reconciliation date, what is the comparative effect on the two books?
Option A: Pass Book balance will be higher than the balance as per Cash Book
Option B: Pass Book will show an overdraft, while Cash Book shows zero
Option C: Cash Book balance will be higher than the balance as per Pass Book
Option D: Both balances will decrease immediately
Hint: Issuing a cheque immediately credits (deducts) the Cash Book, but the bank has not yet debited (deducted) it.
Explanation: Section 6.3(I)(a)(i) states: 'As soon as a cheque is issued, it is entered on the credit side of the Cash Book but the bank makes no entry for cheque until it is presented for payment... the balance in the Pass Book will be higher than the balance as per Cash Book on that date.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: When cheques are deposited into the bank but not yet cleared and collected by the bank, what is the relative state of the two balances?
Option A: Pass Book balance is higher than Cash Book balance
Option B: Both books show identical balances
Option C: Cash Book balance is higher than Pass Book balance
Option D: Cash Book reflects a credit balance and Pass Book reflects an overdraft
Hint: Depositing a cheque immediately debits (increases) the Cash Book, but the bank credits it only after clearing.
Explanation: Section 6.3(I)(a)(ii) states: 'As soon as cheques are received and deposited... they are recorded in the Cash Book on debit side which increase the balance at bank as per Cash Book but bank does not give credit... until it is cleared and collected... Therefore, balance as per Cash Book is higher.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: When the bank credits interest on deposit in the Pass Book, what is the effect on the balances before the customer receives intimation?
Option A: Both books reflect an automatic overdraft
Option B: Cash Book balance is higher than Pass Book balance
Option C: Pass Book balance remains unchanged while Cash Book increases
Option D: Pass Book balance is higher than Cash Book balance
Hint: Interest credited by the bank increases the funds in the bank account first.
Explanation: Section 6.3(I)(b)(i) states: 'If the bank allows interest to customer it credits the customer account and the bank balance as per Pass Book will increase... Until then the balance as per Pass Book would be more than the balance as per Cash Book.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: When a bank collects dividend, interest, or rent directly on behalf of a customer under standing instructions, why does a difference arise?
Option A: Because the bank credits the customer's account immediately, but the customer enters it in the Cash Book only upon receiving the statement or advice
Option B: Because the Cash Book must record dividend only at the end of the financial year
Option C: Because dividend collection is illegal without prior court sanction
Option D: Because the bank debits the customer's account without sending an advice
Hint: The money enters the bank first; the customer learns of it only when reviewing bank statements or SMS.
Explanation: Section 6.3(I)(b)(ii) explains that the bank collects and credits the customer's account directly, increasing the Pass Book balance. The customer records it in the Cash Book only upon receiving the statement/intimation, creating a timing difference where Pass Book > Cash Book.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: When the bank pays insurance premiums, electricity bills, or loan instalments under standing instructions, what is the effect on relative balances before intimation?
Option A: Cash Book balance will decrease automatically without any intimation
Option B: Pass Book balance will be less than Cash Book balance
Option C: Pass Book will reflect an overcast balance
Option D: Pass Book balance will be higher than Cash Book balance
Hint: Direct payment deducts money from the bank account before the firm's accountant records it.
Explanation: Section 6.3(I)(b)(iii) states: 'As soon as such payments are made bank debits customer account in bank Pass Book / bank statement but the customer has no information... Till then balance as per Pass Book / bank statement will be less than balance as per Cash Book.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: How do bank charges, commission, and interest on overdraft debited by the bank affect the Pass Book balance on the reconciliation date?
Option A: They cause Pass Book balance to be higher than Cash Book balance
Option B: They have no effect on either book balance
Option C: They increase the cash column of the Cash Book
Option D: They cause Pass Book balance to be less than Cash Book balance
Hint: Debits in the Pass Book represent deductions made by the bank.
Explanation: Section 6.3(I)(b)(iv) states: 'Bank debits the customer's account for such facilities time to time. However, the firm will know about these charges... only when it goes through the bank Pass Book... So, on the date of reconciliation balance as per Pass Book will be less than that of Cash Book.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: When a customer's debtor deposits money directly into the businessman's bank account via NEFT or cash, what is the effect on the two books before the bank statement is received?
Option A: Balance shown in Pass Book will be more than balance shown in Cash Book
Option B: The debtor's personal account in the business ledger is automatically credited by the bank
Option C: Balance shown in Cash Book will be more than balance shown in Pass Book
Option D: Cash Book will show a credit balance while Pass Book shows zero
Hint: The deposit is already sitting in the bank account, but unentered in the Cash Book.
Explanation: Section 6.3(I)(b)(vi) states: 'bank records the receipt in customers account but the same is not recorded in the businessman's Cash Book. As a result, the balance shown in bank Pass Book will be more than the balance shown in Cash Book.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: When a bill of exchange discounted with the bank is dishonoured on the due date, what entry does the bank make in the Pass Book?
Option A: Bank debits the customer's account in the Pass Book
Option B: Bank issues a new bill of exchange automatically
Option C: Bank writes off the bill against its statutory bad debt reserves
Option D: Bank credits the customer's account to return the discount charge
Hint: The bank recovers the unpaid funds from the customer who discounted the bill.
Explanation: Section 6.3(I)(b)(v) states: 'When cheque or Bill of exchange discounted with the bank is dishonoured, the same is debited in the Pass Book / bank statement but not given effect in the Cash Book until intimation is received.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: If a cheque issued by a businessman to make a payment is returned dishonoured, how does the bank cancel the earlier debit entry in the Pass Book?
Option A: Bank deletes the transaction from the electronic database completely
Option B: Bank credits the customer's account in the Pass Book
Option C: Bank debits the customer's account a second time
Option D: Bank freezes the customer's overdraft facility permanently
Hint: To reverse a previous debit, what accounting entry must be passed?
Explanation: Section 6.3(I)(b)(v) explains: 'when customer makes the payment by cheque and if it is dishonoured, bank credits the same in Pass Book / bank statement to cancel the earlier effect of cheque but will not give effect of dishonour of cheque in the Cash Book until the intimation is received.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Bank charges of Rs 540 debited by the bank were mistakenly entered in the Cash Book as Rs 450. What type of cause of discrepancy does this illustrate?
Option A: Omission of a transaction by the bank
Option B: Statutory deduction of tax at source
Option C: Error committed by the businessman in recording the wrong amount
Option D: Timing difference due to clearing delay
Hint: Look at the specific numerical illustration given in Section 6.3(ii) on page 185.
Explanation: Section 6.3(ii) cites this exact example: 'Differences in balance may also arise due to errors committed by bank or businessman. For example, bank charges debited by bank 540 is recorded as 450 in Cash Book. Here the transaction appears in both the books but with wrong amount.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: A customer deposit of Rs 26,200 into the bank was mistakenly entered in the CASH column instead of the BANK column of the Cash Book. What is the effect on the Bank Reconciliation Statement?
Option A: It creates no difference in the Bank Reconciliation Statement
Option B: The Cash Book bank column omitted this deposit, so the Cash Book bank balance is Rs 26,200 lower than the Pass Book
Option C: The Pass Book balance is Rs 26,200 lower than the Cash Book bank balance
Option D: The cash in hand is understated by Rs 26,200
Hint: See Illustration 10 Item (iii): The bank collected the deposit, but the Cash Book BANK column did not record it.
Explanation: Because the cash deposit was entered in the cash column rather than the bank column, the bank column of the Cash Book failed to reflect the deposit. The bank credited it in the Pass Book, so the Cash Book bank balance is Rs 26,200 lower than the Pass Book balance.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: A cheque of Rs 4,250 received from Akash was deposited into the bank for collection but was NOT yet collected by the bank. The accountant mistakenly recorded the entry in the CASH column of the Cash Book. Why does this item NOT appear in the BRS?
Option A: Because cheques under Rs 5,000 are exempt from reconciliation
Option B: Because the cheque was issued by a debtor rather than a supplier
Option C: Because it was omitted from the Cash Book bank column and has also not yet been credited in the Pass Book, thus creating zero difference between the two bank records
Option D: Because cash transactions are strictly prohibited from being reconciled
Hint: Review the Note to Illustration 7: Does the transaction appear in either bank account record?
Explanation: As noted in Illustration 7 (Note to Item vi): 'This does not create any difference in the balance of the two books because it has not been recorded in the Bank column of cash-book and it does not appear in the Pass Book too since it has not been collected by bank.' Hence no discrepancy exists between the two bank balances.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: If the debit (receipt) side of the bank column in the Cash Book is overcast by Rs 100, what is the direct effect on the Cash Book balance?
Option A: The Pass Book balance is overstated by Rs 100
Option B: The Cash Book bank balance is overstated by Rs 100
Option C: The Pass Book overdraft is reduced by Rs 100
Option D: The Cash Book bank balance is understated by Rs 100
Hint: Overcasting means calculating a column total higher than its true sum.
Explanation: Overcasting receipts (debit side) of the Cash Book inflates total receipts, thereby artificially overstating the closing Cash Book bank balance by Rs 100 relative to the true bank balance.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: What is the effect on the Cash Book balance if the credit (payment) side of the bank column in the Cash Book is undercast by Rs 350?
Option A: Cash Book balance is overstated by Rs 350
Option B: Pass Book overdraft increases by Rs 350
Option C: Pass Book balance is understated by Rs 350
Option D: Cash Book balance is understated by Rs 350
Hint: Undercasting payments means total deductions are smaller than they should be.
Explanation: When the payment side is undercast, payments are totalled to a smaller sum than actual. Deducting less from receipts causes the resulting Cash Book closing balance to be overstated (higher) by Rs 350.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: If the debit (withdrawal) side of the Bank Pass Book is overcast by Rs 300, how does this affect the Pass Book balance?
Option A: Pass Book balance is understated by Rs 300
Option B: Cash Book balance is understated by Rs 300
Option C: Pass Book balance is overstated by Rs 300
Option D: Pass Book reflects a zero balance
Hint: Pass Book debit side records withdrawals. Adding them up too high deducts too much from the account.
Explanation: Pass Book debit entries represent withdrawals. If total withdrawals are overcast (totalled too high by Rs 300), the calculated Pass Book balance will be understated by Rs 300 (or the overdraft will be overstated by Rs 300).

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: If the credit (receipt) side of the Bank Pass Book is undercast by Rs 1,000, what is the effect on the Pass Book balance?
Option A: Pass Book balance is overstated by Rs 1,000
Option B: Pass Book reflects an unpresented cheque of Rs 1,000
Option C: Pass Book balance is understated by Rs 1,000
Option D: Cash Book balance is understated by Rs 1,000
Hint: Undercasting deposits means showing fewer total deposits than actually occurred.
Explanation: The credit side of the Pass Book records deposits. If this side is undercast by Rs 1,000, total deposits are short by Rs 1,000, causing the Pass Book balance to be understated by Rs 1,000.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: An electricity bill of Rs 6,200 paid directly by the bank was erroneously debited TWICE in the Pass Book. What is the effect on the Pass Book balance?
Option A: Pass Book balance is understated by Rs 12,400
Option B: Cash Book balance is understated by Rs 6,200
Option C: Pass Book balance is overstated by Rs 6,200
Option D: Pass Book balance is understated by Rs 6,200
Hint: The bank subtracted Rs 6,200 one extra time.
Explanation: Because the bank debited the Rs 6,200 payment twice instead of once, an extra deduction of Rs 6,200 was made from the customer's account, causing the Pass Book balance to be understated by Rs 6,200.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: A business proprietor purchased furniture for Rs 25,000 and paid using a business debit card. The accountant omitted to enter this payment in the Cash Book. What is the effect on the Cash Book balance?
Option A: Cash Book balance remains overstated by Rs 25,000 compared to the actual bank balance
Option B: Cash Book balance is understated by Rs 25,000
Option C: Pass Book balance is overstated by Rs 25,000
Option D: Cash Book reflects an automatic overdraft of Rs 25,000
Hint: Money left the bank via the card swipe, but the Cash Book has not subtracted it.
Explanation: A debit card payment is debited immediately by the bank in the Pass Book. Since it was omitted from the Cash Book, the Cash Book has not subtracted the Rs 25,000, leaving its balance higher (overstated) than the Pass Book by Rs 25,000.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: A cheque of Rs 1,500 issued to a supplier ABC & Co. by business debit card was recorded on the payment side of the Cash Book as Rs 150. What is the resulting error in the Cash Book balance?
Option A: Cash Book balance is understated by Rs 1,350
Option B: Cash Book balance is understated by Rs 150
Option C: Cash Book balance is overstated by Rs 1,350
Option D: Pass Book balance is overstated by Rs 1,350
Hint: Actual payment deducted by bank = Rs 1,500; payment deducted in Cash Book = only Rs 150.
Explanation: The bank deducted the full Rs 1,500, but the Cash Book subtracted only Rs 150 (short deduction of Rs 1,350). By subtracting Rs 1,350 less than actual, the Cash Book balance remains overstated by Rs 1,350.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: A cheque of Rs 975 deposited into the bank was correctly credited by the bank, but entered on the debit side of the Cash Book as Rs 795. What is the effect on the Cash Book balance?
Option A: Cash Book balance is overstated by Rs 180
Option B: Cash Book balance is understated by Rs 180
Option C: Cash Book balance is understated by Rs 975
Option D: Pass Book balance is understated by Rs 180
Hint: Actual receipt = Rs 975; receipt entered in Cash Book = Rs 795. The debit was short by Rs 180.
Explanation: The Cash Book recorded a receipt of Rs 795 instead of Rs 975 (975 - 795 = 180 short). Entering a smaller receipt causes the Cash Book balance to be understated by Rs 180 compared to the Pass Book.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Why is the last day of the month generally selected for preparing a Bank Reconciliation Statement?
Option A: Because commercial banks close all business current accounts on that day
Option B: Because banking laws make reconciliation invalid if done mid-month
Option C: Because interest on fixed deposits is calculated strictly every 30 days
Option D: Because Cash Book balance and Pass Book balance are readily available on that date
Hint: Refer to Step 5 of the preparation procedure in Section 6.5.
Explanation: Section 6.5 Step 5 explicitly states: 'The date for the preparation of the Bank Reconciliation Statement is generally chosen as the last day of the month because Cash Book balance and Pass Book balance are readily available on that date.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: In the alternative Plus (+) and Minus (-) column method of preparing BRS, in which column is a 'Credit balance as per Pass Book' entered?
Option A: Suspense column
Option B: Overdraft column only
Option C: Plus (+) column
Option D: Minus (-) column
Hint: In the Pass Book, a credit balance represents deposits belonging to the customer (favourable).
Explanation: Under 'Alternate Presentation' in Section 6.4: 'Credit balance of Pass Book is written in plus column. Debit balance of Pass Book or overdraft is written in minus column.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: In the alternative Plus and Minus method, where is an 'Overdraft as per Cash Book' (credit balance) recorded?
Option A: Minus (-) column
Option B: It is omitted until the end of the year
Option C: Plus (+) column
Option D: Both Plus and Minus columns equally
Hint: An overdraft in the Cash Book is a credit balance (unfavourable).
Explanation: Section 6.4 specifies: 'Credit balance of Cash Book or overdraft is written in minus column. Debit balance of Cash Book is written in plus column.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: According to the general rule of plus and minus in Section 6.5, when 'Bank Balance as per Cash Book' is given as the starting point, what is the rule for adjustments?
Option A: Add all Pass Book entries; ignore Cash Book entries
Option B: Add debits in Cash Book or in Pass Book; Less credits in Cash Book or in Pass Book
Option C: Add credits in Cash Book or in Pass Book; Less debits in Cash Book or in Pass Book
Option D: Deduct credits and add debits
Hint: Review Step 8(a) of Section 6.5.
Explanation: Section 6.5 Step 8(a) states: 'When balance as per Cash Book is given: Add credits in Cash Book or in Pass Book; Less debits in Cash Book or in Pass Book.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: According to Section 6.5 Step 8(b), when 'Bank Balance as per Pass Book' is given as the starting point, how are adjustments made?
Option A: Add only unpresented cheques and deduct direct collections
Option B: Add credits in Cash Book or in Pass Book; Less debits in Cash Book or in Pass Book
Option C: Add debits in Cash Book or in Pass Book; Less credits in Cash Book or in Pass Book
Option D: Add uncleared deposits and add direct payments
Hint: Pass Book balance behaves oppositely to Cash Book balance.
Explanation: Section 6.5 Step 8(b) explicitly provides: 'When balance as per Pass Book is given: Add debits in Cash Book or in Pass Book; Less credits in Cash Book or in Pass Book.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: When 'Overdraft as per Cash Book' is the starting point in a BRS, what is the adjustment rule prescribed in Step 8(c)?
Option A: Add debits in Cash Book or in Pass Book; Less credits in Cash Book or in Pass Book
Option B: Deduct all bank charges and add interest allowed
Option C: Add unpresented cheques and deduct uncredited cheques
Option D: Add credits in Cash Book or in Pass Book; Less debits in Cash Book or in Pass Book
Hint: Overdraft as per Cash Book follows the opposite rule of normal Cash Book balance.
Explanation: Section 6.5 Step 8(c) states: 'When overdraft as per Cash Book is given: Add debits in Cash Book or in Pass Book; Less credits in Cash Book or in Pass Book.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: When 'Overdraft as per Pass Book' is given as the starting point, what is the adjustment rule under Step 8(d)?
Option A: Deduct all dishonoured cheques and deduct bank charges
Option B: Add debits in Cash Book or in Pass Book; Less credits in Cash Book or in Pass Book
Option C: Add credits in Cash Book or in Pass Book; Less debits in Cash Book or in Pass Book
Option D: Add uncredited cheques and add standing order payments
Hint: Overdraft as per Pass Book follows the same rule as normal Cash Book balance.
Explanation: Section 6.5 Step 8(d) states: 'When overdraft as per Pass Book is given: Add credits in Cash Book or in Pass Book; Less debits in Cash Book or in Pass Book.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: When extracts of Cash Book and Pass Book are provided for a COMMON period (e.g., both for October 2018), which items must be considered to prepare the BRS?
Option A: All transactions from both books without exception
Option B: Only opening balances of both books
Option C: Only uncommon (unticked) items that appear in one book but not the other
Option D: Only common items appearing in both books
Hint: See Section 6.5(A): Items appearing in both books during the same month do not create differences.
Explanation: Section 6.5(A) states: 'Entries appearing in both the books in the same period do not create any difference in the balance of the two books, thus are to be ignored. The items which appear in Cash Book but does not appear in Pass Book and vice versa will only create difference... These are entered in the Bank Reconciliation Statement.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: When extracts of Cash Book and Pass Book are given for UNCOMMON / DIFFERENT periods (e.g., Cash Book for January and Pass Book for February), which items create discrepancies for the BRS as on 31st January?
Option A: Opening balances only
Option B: All transactions recorded in February Pass Book that do not appear in January Cash Book
Option C: Only uncommon items appearing solely in the January Cash Book
Option D: Only the common items appearing in both books
Hint: Refer to Section 6.5(B) and Exercise Q.4(9).
Explanation: Section 6.5(B) explicitly states: 'When extract is given for uncommon period, consider only common items appearing in both the books. Common items only create discrepancies in the balance of the two books which are to be adjusted in the Bank Reconciliation Statement.' (Because appearing in February proves they were pending on 31st January).

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: The bank balance as per Cash Book is Rs 22,380 as on 30th April 2019. Cheques issued to Atul & Sons of Rs 2,600 were not presented for payment. Dividend of Rs 2,000 collected by the bank appeared in the Pass Book only. Cheques deposited but not collected amounted to Rs 13,900. Insurance premium paid by bank was Rs 6,500 and bank charges were Rs 800 (neither recorded in Cash Book). What is the Bank Balance as per Pass Book?
Hint: Review Illustration 1: Starting Cash Book balance 22,380 + additions (2,600 + 2,000) - deductions (13,900 + 6,500 + 800).
Explanation: Starting balance = Rs 22,380. Add: Cheque unpresented (Rs 2,600) + Dividend collected (Rs 2,000) = Rs 4,600. Total = Rs 26,980. Less: Cheques uncollected (Rs 13,900) + Insurance premium (Rs 6,500) + Bank charges (Rs 800) = Rs 21,200. Bank balance as per Pass Book = 26,980 - 21,200 = Rs 5,780.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: On 31st January 2019, Cash Book bank balance was Rs 81,000. Cheques issued to Hemant (Rs 19,500), Pravin (Rs 9,900), and Vidya (Rs 27,000) were not presented for payment in January. Cheques deposited for Sangeeta (Rs 75,000) and Shruti (Rs 24,000) were cleared by the bank only in February. What was the Bank Balance as per Pass Book on 31st January 2019?
Hint: Review Illustration 2: Starting balance 81,000 + unpresented cheques 56,400 - uncleared cheques 99,000.
Explanation: Starting balance as per Cash Book = Rs 81,000. Add unpresented cheques: 19,500 + 9,900 + 27,000 = Rs 56,400. Total = Rs 1,37,400. Less uncleared cheques: 75,000 + 24,000 = Rs 99,000. Balance as per Pass Book = 1,37,400 - 99,000 = Rs 38,400.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question:
The Cash Book shows a bank balance of Rs 57,400 as on 31st March 2019. Discrepancies identified include:
- Cheque of Rs 6,350 deposited but not collected
- Electricity bill paid by bank Rs 9,700 (not in Cash Book)
- Cheque issued Rs 15,100 not presented
- Interest on investment collected by bank Rs 8,800 (not in Cash Book)
- Bank charges Rs 650 debited in Pass Book
- Debtor Tanmay directly deposited Rs 12,000 into bank
What is the Bank balance as per Pass Book?
Explanation: Cash Book balance = Rs 57,400. Additions: Cheque unpresented (15,100) + Interest collected (8,800) + Direct deposit (12,000) = Rs 35,900. Total = Rs 93,300. Deductions: Cheque uncollected (6,350) + Electricity bill (9,700) + Bank charges (650) = Rs 16,700. Bank balance as per Pass Book = 93,300 - 16,700 = Rs 76,600.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question:
From the following details, find the Bank Balance as per Cash Book as on 30th June 2019:
- Balance as per Pass Book: Rs 14,000
- Cheques deposited Rs 16,400, but only Rs 6,400 cleared (Rs 10,000 uncleared)
- Cash withdrawn for personal use Rs 5,500 not in Cash Book
- Bank incidental charges Rs 350 debited in Pass Book only
- Cheque dishonoured debited in Pass Book only Rs 7,500
- Two cheques of Rs 8,900 and Rs 10,700 issued, but only Rs 8,900 presented (Rs 10,700 unpresented)
- Interest credited in Pass Book only Rs 425
Hint: Review Illustration 4: Pass Book balance 14,000 + Additions (10,000 + 5,500 + 350 + 7,500 = 23,350) - Deductions (10,700 + 425 = 11,125).
Explanation: Pass Book balance = Rs 14,000. Add debits: Cheque uncleared (10,000) + Drawings omitted in Cash Book (5,500) + Incidental charges (350) + Cheque dishonoured (7,500) = Rs 23,350. Total = Rs 37,350. Less credits: Unpresented cheque (10,700) + Interest credited (425) = Rs 11,125. Balance as per Cash Book = 37,350 - 11,125 = Rs 26,225.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question:
Cash Book of Kunal showed an Overdraft of Rs 36,280 on 31st July 2019. The differences include:
- Direct deposit by customer Manish: Rs 18,700
- Cheque of Rs 18,900 deposited was debited in Cash Book as Rs 19,800 (excess debit Rs 900)
- Cheque issued for salary Rs 25,000 presented in August
- Cash withdrawn from ATM for office use Rs 20,000 not in Cash Book
- Debit side of Cash Book overcast by Rs 100
- Office rent paid by bank Rs 19,500
- Commission collected by bank Rs 3,750
What is the Bank Overdraft as per Pass Book?
Hint: Review Illustration 5: Overdraft as per Cash Book 36,280 + Add (900 + 20,000 + 100 + 19,500 = 40,500) - Less (18,700 + 25,000 + 3,750 = 47,450).
Explanation: Starting Overdraft = Rs 36,280. Add items that increase overdraft: Excess debit in CB (900) + ATM withdrawal omitted (20,000) + Overcast of CB debit (100) + Office rent paid (19,500) = Rs 40,500. Total = Rs 76,780. Less items that decrease overdraft: Direct deposit (18,700) + Cheque unpresented (25,000) + Commission collected (3,750) = Rs 47,450. Overdraft as per Pass Book = 76,780 - 47,450 = Rs 29,330.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question:
Pass Book of Mr. Bhuvaneshwar shows an Overdraft of Rs 53,970 on 31st Oct 2018. Discrepancies:
- Wrong credit given by bank in Pass Book: Rs 17,070
- Cheques issued but not presented: Rs 40,000
- Annual subscription paid by bank not in Cash Book: Rs 6,000
- Payment side of Cash Book undercast: Rs 350
- Interest on overdraft charged: Rs 1,530
- Cash deposit of Rs 23,000 not recorded in Pass Book
What is the Bank Overdraft as per Cash Book?
Hint: Review Illustration 6: Starting Overdraft as per Pass Book 53,970 + Add (17,070 + 40,000 = 57,070) - Less (6,000 + 350 + 1,530 + 23,000 = 30,880).
Explanation: Overdraft as per Pass Book = Rs 53,970. Add credits in Pass Book/Cash Book: Wrong credit in PB (17,070) + Unpresented cheques (40,000) = Rs 57,070. Total = Rs 1,11,040. Less debits: Subscription paid (6,000) + Undercast CB payment (350) + Interest on overdraft (1,530) + Deposit uncredited (23,000) = Rs 30,880. Overdraft as per Cash Book = 1,11,040 - 30,880 = Rs 80,160.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question:
Cash Book of Pankaj shows a credit balance (overdraft) of Rs 32,490 on 30th Sept 2018. Discrepancies:
- Cheques deposited Rs 36,000, only Rs 11,360 credited (Rs 24,640 uncleared)
- Cheques issued but unencashed: Rs 93,000
- Cheque book charges Rs 250 & SMS alert charges Rs 170 in Pass Book only
- Customer NEFT transfer Rs 1,23,200 entered in Cash Book as Rs 12,320 (Rs 1,10,880 under-recorded)
- Receipt side of Pass Book undercast by Rs 1,000
- Dividend collected by bank: Rs 12,500
What is the final bank position as per Pass Book?
Option A: Overdraft of Rs 58,550
Option B: Favourable Bank balance of Rs 32,490
Option C: Overdraft of Rs 1,57,830
Option D: Favourable Bank balance of Rs 1,57,830
Hint: Review Illustration 8: Overdraft 32,490 + Additions (26,060) = 58,550. Deductions = 93,000 + 1,10,880 + 12,500 = 2,16,380. Because deductions exceed the overdraft, it becomes a positive credit balance.
Explanation: Starting Overdraft as per Cash Book = Rs 32,490. Add items increasing overdraft: Uncleared cheques (24,640) + Cheque book charges (250) + SMS charges (170) + Undercast PB receipt (1,000) = Rs 26,060. Total minus items = Rs 58,550. Less items reducing overdraft: Unpresented cheques (93,000) + Excess NEFT receipt (1,10,880) + Dividend (12,500) = Rs 2,16,380. Net result = 58,550 - 2,16,380 = - Rs 1,57,830. A negative result converts overdraft into a favourable Bank Balance as per Pass Book of Rs 1,57,830.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question:
Bank Pass Book of Mr. Ravi showed a credit balance of Rs 16,700 on 31st March 2018. Discrepancies:
- Cheques deposited Rs 27,000, only Rs 23,000 credited (Rs 4,000 uncleared)
- Discounted Bill Receivable dishonoured: Rs 11,700
- Pass Book debit side overcast: Rs 300
- Savings cash Rs 8,500 drawn shown under current account in Cash Book
- Cheques issued Rs 40,500, only Rs 1,500 presented (Rs 39,000 unpresented)
- Insurance premium Rs 14,400 entered twice in Cash Book
- Interest allowed by bank Rs 800 in Pass Book only
What is the Bank Overdraft as per Cash Book?
Hint: Review Illustration 9: Balance as per Pass Book 16,700 + Additions (4,000 + 11,700 + 300 = 16,000) = 32,700. Deductions (8,500 + 39,000 + 14,400 + 800 = 62,700). Difference = 32,700 - 62,700 = -30,000.
Explanation: Pass Book balance = Rs 16,700. Add debits in PB/CB: Uncleared cheques (4,000) + Dishonoured bill (11,700) + Overcast PB debit (300) = Rs 16,000. Total = Rs 32,700. Less credits: Savings withdrawal in CB (8,500) + Unpresented cheques (39,000) + Duplicate insurance debit in CB (14,400) + Interest allowed (800) = Rs 62,700. Net result = 32,700 - 62,700 = - Rs 30,000. Negative answer converts favourable balance into Bank Overdraft as per Cash Book of Rs 30,000.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: What is the primary definition and concept of Vendor Reconciliation (reconciliation of debtors and creditors)?
Option A: Verifying the physical inventory count in the vendor's warehouse
Option B: Verifying the completeness and accuracy of accounting records by comparing the debtor's ledger in our books with our ledger in the debtor's books to identify and fix errors
Option C: Reconciling bank accounts with currency reserves held by foreign suppliers
Option D: Negotiating new credit periods and cash discounts with trade associations
Hint: Read the opening paragraph under 'Reconciliation of Debtors and Creditors' on page 202.
Explanation: The text explains: 'Reconciliation helps us to identify and fix accounting errors. Reconciliation is carried out to verify the completeness and accuracy of a particular part of accounting records by comparing it with another record. Reconciliation Statement can also be prepared for vendor reconciliation i.e. reconciliation of debtors and creditors. Debtors represent money owed to us and creditors represent money owed by us. Here we compare debtor's ledger in our books with our ledger in the debtor's book and reconcile the differences if any.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: What is the precise procedural sequence followed for Reconciliation of Debtors and Creditors as detailed in Section 6.5?
Option A: Prepare reconciliation statement -> Group differences -> Request debtor's ledger -> File a recovery lawsuit -> Send demand notice
Option B: Sum all invoices -> Deduct cash receipts -> Post the net figure to capital reserve
Option C: Write off unmatched items to bad debts -> Inform bank manager -> Close debtor's ledger account
Option D: Request counterparty ledger -> Prepare our ledger in Excel -> Copy-paste into one Excel file -> Compare and match entries -> List non-matching items -> Group differences -> Prepare reconciliation statement
Hint: Review the 7 numbered steps on page 202 under 'Procedure for Reconciliation of Debtors and Creditors'.
Explanation: The chapter lists the 7 steps: 1. Request debtor to give our ledger account in their books, 2. Prepare debtor's ledger in Excel, 3. Copy-paste both in one Excel file, 4. Compare and match entries, 5. Prepare list for non-matching entries, 6. Group similar differences and give headings, 7. Prepare vendor reconciliation statement. The correct option matches this exact chronological workflow.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: In financial terms as stated in the chapter, what do 'Debtors' and 'Creditors' represent respectively?
Option A: Debtors represent money owed by us; Creditors represent money owed to us
Option B: Debtors represent long-term bank loans; Creditors represent cash deposited with banks
Option C: Debtors represent statutory tax obligations; Creditors represent prepaid expenses
Option D: Debtors represent money owed to us; Creditors represent money owed by us
Hint: Check the exact sentence under Section 6.5 on page 202 defining both terms.
Explanation: The chapter explicitly defines: 'Debtors represent money owed to us and creditors represent money owed by us.' The other options reverse these fundamental roles or misclassify them as loans or taxes.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: A business issued a cheque of Rs 20,000 to a creditor, but only Rs 8,000 was presented to the bank before month-end. When preparing BRS starting with 'Bank balance as per Cash Book', how much is added?
Hint: Only the unpresented portion causes a disagreement between the two books.
Explanation: Out of Rs 20,000 issued, Rs 8,000 was presented and cleared in both books. Only the unpresented portion of Rs 12,000 (20,000 - 8,000) causes a difference, and is added to the Cash Book balance.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Cheques sent to bank for collection totaled Rs 2,00,000, out of which cheques of Rs 80,000 only were credited by the bank during the month. When reconciling starting from 'Bank balance as per Cash Book', what amount should be deducted?
Hint: Deduct only the uncredited portion that has not yet appeared in the Pass Book.
Explanation: Total deposited = Rs 2,00,000. Credited by bank = Rs 80,000. The amount not yet credited is Rs 1,20,000 (2,00,000 - 80,000). Starting from Cash Book balance, uncleared cheques of Rs 1,20,000 must be deducted.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: A customer's debtor directly deposited Rs 1,500 into the bank account, but the accountant mistakenly recorded the transaction in the CASH column of the Cash Book. How should this be treated when reconciling starting from 'Overdraft as per Cash Book'?
Option A: It is deducted from the overdraft as a credit not entered in the Cash Book bank column
Option B: It is added to the overdraft because it was recorded in the Cash Book
Option C: It is ignored completely because the cash column was already debited
Option D: It is treated as a dishonoured cheque and debited to the debtor
Hint: Look at Practical Problem 9 Item 7: The bank column in the Cash Book omitted the deposit, so the bank received funds that reduce the overdraft.
Explanation: Recording the receipt in the cash column means the bank column of the Cash Book has no record of the Rs 1,500 deposit. The bank credited it in the Pass Book, reducing the overdraft. When starting from Overdraft as per Cash Book, credits in the Pass Book reduce the overdraft and must be deducted (Less item).

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Under standing instructions, the bank transferred Rs 2,500 from the business current account to the personal savings account of the proprietor, but no entry was made in the Cash Book. How is this treated when reconciling starting from 'Overdraft as per Cash Book'?
Option A: Ignored because it represents proprietor's drawings
Option B: Multiplied by two and subtracted
Option C: Deducted from the overdraft
Option D: Added to the overdraft
Hint: The bank debited the current account for Rs 2,500, increasing the overdraft at the bank.
Explanation: The bank transfer is a withdrawal (debit) from the current account, increasing the bank overdraft. The Cash Book has not recorded this payment. Starting with Overdraft as per Cash Book, debits in the Pass Book must be ADDED to arrive at the Pass Book overdraft.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: A Bill of Exchange for Rs 3,500 discounted with the bank in December 2018 returned dishonoured in January 2019. When preparing the Bank Reconciliation Statement as on 31st December 2018, how should this bill be treated?
Option A: It will NOT appear in the December 2018 BRS because the dishonour occurred after 31st December 2018
Option B: It must be deducted as an unpresented cheque
Option C: It must be added to both Cash Book and Pass Book balances
Option D: It must be debited to the Pass Book in the December BRS
Hint: Look at Practical Problem 10 Item 5: Check the exact date of dishonour relative to the reconciliation date.
Explanation: On 31st December 2018, the bill had not yet been dishonoured (it was dishonoured in January 2019). As on 31st December 2018, neither the bank nor the Cash Book had any entry for dishonour, so no discrepancy existed on that date.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: In Exercise Q.2, what single accounting term is defined as: 'Excess of bank deposits over withdrawals by businessman in bank current account'?
Option A: Bank Balance (Favourable Balance)
Option B: Bank Overdraft
Option C: Cash Credit
Option D: Capital Reserve
Hint: When deposits exceed withdrawals, the customer has positive funds in the bank.
Explanation: Exercise Q.2(10) defines: 'Excess of bank deposits over withdrawals by businessman in bank current account' as Bank Balance (or Favourable Bank Balance). When withdrawals exceed deposits, it is an overdraft.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: In Exercise Q.4, what happens when an entry is debited in the Cash Book?
Option A: It cancels previous receipts
Option B: It increases the cash/bank balance
Option C: It creates an automatic overdraft
Option D: It decreases the cash/bank balance
Hint: Cash Book is an asset account: debits represent receipts.
Explanation: Exercise Q.4(4) states: 'Debiting an entry in Cash Book increases cash balance.' (Since Cash Book is an asset account where receipts are debited).

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Which type of bank account holder is granted the 'Bank Overdraft' facility by commercial banks?
Option A: Fixed deposit account holder
Option B: Current account holder
Option C: Recurring deposit account holder
Option D: Savings account holder
Hint: Refer to Exercise Q.4(7) and Section 6.1(4).
Explanation: Exercise Q.4(7) states: 'Bank gives overdraft facility to Current account holder.' Overdraft facilities are not provided on standard savings or recurring accounts.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Payments credited in the Cash Book are recorded on which side of the Bank Pass Book?
Option A: Entered in the particulars column only
Option B: Debited in Pass Book
Option C: Credited in Pass Book
Option D: Ignored in Pass Book
Hint: Look at Exercise Q.5(1): 'Payments credited in Cash Book are _____ in Pass Book.'
Explanation: Payments credited in the Cash Book represent withdrawals from the bank account. When the bank clears and pays these amounts, it debits the customer's account in the Pass Book.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: While preparing a Bank Reconciliation Statement, which specific column of the Cash Book is considered?
Option A: Bank column only
Option B: Both Cash and Bank columns combined
Option C: Discount column only
Option D: Cash column only
Hint: Exercise Q.5(2): 'While preparing Bank Reconciliation Statement only _____ column of Cash Book is considered.'
Explanation: BRS specifically reconciles banking transactions between the bank column of the Cash Book and the Pass Book. The cash and discount columns are excluded.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: When a cheque is issued to a creditor, in which book does the entry appear FIRST?
Option A: Cash Book
Option B: Bank Advice
Option C: Pass Book
Option D: Sales Day Book
Hint: Exercise Q.5(3): 'Cheques issued to creditors appear first in _____ book.'
Explanation: As soon as a businessman writes and signs a cheque to a creditor, it is immediately entered on the credit side of the Cash Book. It appears in the Pass Book only later when the creditor presents it for clearing.
